utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Taraba. Let us continue where we left off yesterday. We were talking about paragraph 3.2. Mr. Taraba, who called you up on the 15th of April, 1993, at night?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My late colleague, Ivan Budimir, rang me up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what function Ivan Budimir was performing at the time?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was a member of the command of the battalion and that he was the assistant commander of the battalion for information and propaganda activity, if I recall rightly. It was IPD.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Regardless of his post, you are sure that he was a member of the command of the battalion of which you were also a member; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what he told you, approximately?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he asked me, "Aren't you in the command? What are you doing?" and I said, "I was sleeping." And he said, "We have to be at the command. You should hurry up and go there."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Mr. Taraba, do you know from where he called you?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he called me from Stara Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was he a resident there?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In Stara Bila itself, or one of the villages near Stara Bila?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a hamlet called Kolotine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you listen to him? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, with great reluctance I got dressed, and I set out toward the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What time was it, approximately, in the night? Early, late?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was about 11.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You said that the command headquarters was in Sumarija, in Rijeka. How far is that from your house, approximately? Either in kilometres or in minutes, driving by car.

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my flat in Vitez, it was about two or two and a half kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Along the way, did you notice anything unusual?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was quiet. It was night; everything was quiet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you notice any movements of soldiers on the road?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you gathered in the command, and my first question is: Did the entire command, did all the members of the command arrive, or just some of them?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say now whether it was everybody who was in the command, but I think it wasn't everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was Mr. Bertovic there when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What did he say to you when you gathered there?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I asked him why they were making us come there, he said that some information had arrived that certain movements of the army of BH had been observed, and that was the reason why he had called the command together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You used the word "again." Your question was, "Why are you making us come here again?" What did you mean by that? Did that happen often?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was, to speak figuratively, the thousandth time. I would come home, take one boot off, and before I could take off the other, the phone would ring and I would have to go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did Bertovic tell you what your task was supposed to be in connection with the information he said he'd received?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said, more or less, that we were to step up measures of observation in the direction of Kruscica and Vranjska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was there any discussion about the entire situation then?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean between me and Mr. Bertovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I mean all of you who were there.

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because I had been so reluctant to come there, I was trying to find a quiet corner where I could nod off and take a nap. I didn't pay any attention to the discussions in the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Before we forget, could you tell us whether Bertovic said quite clearly from whom he had received the information you said he had?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be quite truthful, I never asked him, nor did he tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What was the final decision and command issued by Bertovic after this discussion you mentioned? What was the battalion to do?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in spite of everything, I managed to notice, to observe, that the command was in places facing Kruscica and Vranjska. Part of the men from the shifts who had gone to the front line facing the army of Republika Srpska should go there in case of an attack by units of the army of BH, to defend the lines, to offer resistance, to try to defend the village and to offer resistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that from Kruscica in the direction of the town, there are several routes that could have been taken by an army possibly executing such a plan in order to reach the town?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There are still two good asphalt roads, two roads along which units could move toward Vitez, toward the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were there also natural paths suitable for infantry to go toward the town?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I can say that with certainty because I am a hiker and I had hiked along all those routes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. And was there a similar situation with respect to Vranjska?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Taraba, tell us, please, first of all in your view, what was your opinion about this information and how realistic it was that there might be an attack at that time, that night?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had had information about a possible attack so many times and our people say that if someone is bitten by a snake, he is afraid of a lizard. You don't believe it when you hear that information so many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And did other people feel the same?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from experience, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: According to what you said, you did undertake certain activities to carry out this order; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Otherwise we would have been held responsible for disobeying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, did you think that by posting those groups in some key points you had satisfied the minimum of what the command required; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Taraba, do you remember that at that time in the motel in Kruscica that night, a group of your men was getting ready to take up a shift on the front line against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And do you know, did you let that group know to pull out that night or not?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, that group stayed back in Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Earlier, you told us that at that time you had been supervising the shifts. At that time, for a month before the conflict, is it correct to say that the shift to go to the front would get together at the motel and from there go to the front line?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, by and large, except that with men who would go to the front line to fight against the army of Republika Srpska, I would join them in Vitez, I would board the bus in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. And what happened on the 16th in the morning? Where were you on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 16th of April in the morning, I was in the building of the command of the 1st Battalion, that is the Sumarija building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And after that meeting around midnight, did you ever go home or did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I haven't followed the evidence about the reinforcements or whatever it is at Kruscica. Now, have I understood the evidence right to make sure that I understand it. You're saying, Mr. Taraba, that the order was that the shifts who had been going to the Serb front line should go to Kruscica to defend that line against a possible attack by the BH army. Now, have I understood that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I said that men who were taking shifts to fight the army of Republika Srpska would come back and live at home in their villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't muddle things. Let me understand what the order was. Now, if I am wrong about it, would you explain clearly so we can understand what the order was?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honours. Would you please be so kind and repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What was Mr. Bertovic's order to the command on the night of the 15th, 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He ordered that a group of men who were in those places, in Kruscica that is, the part facing Vranjska to be on the -- to be prepared to be ready because there was information about the movements of the formations of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And as a result of the order, what was done?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should ask Mr. Bertovic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm asking you. You were there, Mr. Taraba. What happened?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe, Your Honour, that some of those men, and I did not check that, were indeed at specific places and undertook some reconnoitring activities so as to prevent a possible attack by the units of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, I can't pretend that it's clear, but we'll go on and perhaps it will become clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will just put one question more. Perhaps it was also my mistake, I was too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It wasn't your mistake. There's some muddle about the troops going to the Serb front line, and I thought it was those units which were ordered to Kruscica, but it doesn't seem that that was the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may remind, those groups in Kruscica motel were mentioned earlier and that is why probably -- but I will put a simple question and I think that the witness will understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Taraba, you mentioned that when there were changes of shifts fighting against the Serbs earlier on, that that group would come back and hand over their weapons after they would return from the shift?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A part of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And that part of a shift, prior to leaving or after returning, would spend a day or a night at a motel in the middle of Kruscica, that is, at the exit from the village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And that critical night, 15th, 16th, did you contact or are you aware if this group was in any way whatsoever covered by this plan of assignments for reconnoitring reinforcements or whatever, was it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Are you sure that there was any such group at that motel at that night at all?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And could you then explain to us, where was that motel in the village? In the middle of the village, on the border of the village or in what direction?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The motel was in the deep rear of the village of Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Let us go back where we were. So in the morning of the 16th of April you were in the Sumarija building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And that morning, was there indeed an attempt of the BH army to attack along any of those directions that you had been put in charge with?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the early morning hours, sometime around 6.00 in the morning, there was general gunfire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Taraba, the Chamber has heard this very many times. I am asking you only about those parts about your area of responsibility. Was there any attempt on the part of the BH army to break through?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know because I have told you that after I had arrived in the command, I was somewhat aloof, indifferent in the situation in the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Taraba, in the morning of the 16th, do you recall any combat operations in that part, in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, combat operations had commenced that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did anything significant happen, a breakthrough, an attempt at a major breakthrough, or not?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That morning, sometime before noon, until 1.00 I spent, probably, I suppose, because of fear and the general state that I was in, under the staircase at the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you mean that you were suffering a kind of a shock that morning?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay with the command, how long after the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: For about four or five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What did you do then?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was trying to help my friends within my powers, Muslims, I need to emphasise, whom I thought might have some problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did you, at that time, request to be transferred to your village?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked the commander to allow me to go to my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When was that, roughly?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said, some four or five days after the beginning of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What was the situation in your village when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a little chaotic. People self-organised -- organised themselves, and fearing the danger that might come from the other side, everyone tried to organise his self-defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At that time when you arrived, could one say that some defence had already been organised? I'm not talking about whether it was good or bad.

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When were the defence sectors formed, approximately? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some six or seven days after the beginning of the conflict, and two or three days after my arrival in my village, the order arrived saying that in order to improve the defence efficiency we should embark upon the organisation of our defence sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, when were all the villagers, I mean all the able-bodied villagers, mobilised?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mobilisation of able-bodied villagers, and later on even those who were not able-bodied, started sometime on the 16th, 17th, 18th, that is, when the conflict intensified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And in your village specifically?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my village, at the very beginning. When I arrived, there was a group of men who seemed to be lost in time and space and yet had organised themselves, and later on, other villages there began to join in one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That "later on," could you specify it? When do you think that the first men were formally mobilised?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first people were formally mobilised sometime on the 16th or the 17th. But I was not in that area so I cannot say exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At the time when the sectors were formed, can we take it that the major part of men were mobilised at that time, in your view, because you were there?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Later on during the war, what are we talking about? When you say "later on," is it a month, two months? When would you say that everybody who could hold a rifle was mobilised?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: By August. Whether it was the end of August -- but by the month of August, even those who were over 65 years of age, and even some 70-year-olds and those who were disabled, were mobilised, that is, practically everybody who could hold a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you roughly define the time when this sectorial defence grew into a different form of organisation and when it became the 2nd Battalion of the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is, I should say, late July, early August, if my memory serves me well. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were you in your village throughout that time?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your village was in the Mosunj defence sector; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the beginning the Mosunj defence sector, and later on the 2nd Battalion of the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did your position change? Your post, did it change after the 2nd Battalion was formed?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you kept your position?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed with the command, but at that time it was the 2nd Battalion of the Vitez Brigade, holding still the same post.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Its headquarters was in your village.

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The headquarters was in Nova Bila, in the neighbourhood community Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Which is how far from your village?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two-hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Taraba, on the eve of the conflict, that is, before the 16th of April, would it be correct to say that there was a core, a nucleus, of the command of the unit that you were a member of?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That nucleus, was it what, in formation terms under the then concept, was to be the battalion command?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In view of your background, you must have had the idea, in formation terms, pursuant to the Territorial Defence concept, you certainly must have been aware of what a battalion command should look like. You did have that knowledge.

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: On the other hand, the situation that you had at that time and how you were organised, was it as that formation should look like, was it worse, or was it better?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was worse, but within our powers, according to what we could do at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did the brigade command already have some organisational nucleus of its command?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thirdly, are you aware - you have already told us, but let us try to support it - that there were lists of military conscripts and those territorially distributed who could be activated and sent to the front line?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In your estimate, since you told us you were involved in all this, how long would it take to activate those men on the lists, that is, to assign them and send them to combat positions? What are we talking about? Is it hours, months, or what?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the former JNA, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, do not --

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise. I merely wanted to draw a parallel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, do go on.

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which was claimed to be a rather well-organised army; its full mobilisation would require 48 hours. And here it was men who lived around in villages, worked in factories which were working at the time, or were employed elsewhere, so that, yes, it took quite some time to mobilise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you give us an example and tell us what you mean by "quite a lot of time"? When you sent shifts to the front, for example - that was mobilisation, in fact - how long did you need beforehand to organise those shifts, to activate the shift for a certain assignment?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean facing the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A week in advance. We would have to organise things a week in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But there was no urgency; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had to replace the shift that was already on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Which meant?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you always did this in a planned fashion. There was no urgency in that sense?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But how would you define -- you said some time, what was the fastest -- how fast could you activate your group of men?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you thinking of the entire battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, for a whole battalion. How long do you think it would take under those circumstances? How soon could you do it, what would be your fastest?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have already said I would need quite some time, which means that if we were talking about a battalion, we would -- that is to say until the end of the conflict, the battalion had not been completed in the sense that was prescribed formation-wise. We never had a complete battalion actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. Mr. Taraba, at that time, you told us what the conditions were and you said that you needed quite some time. Could you make an assessment? What do you mean by that, how much time; several hours, days, several days? So given the prevailing conditions at that time, how much time did you need?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We needed several days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on to another area. We have heard a great deal about the PPN special purpose units that were in the area of the Vitez municipality. Mr. Taraba, my question for you is the following: Did the brigade at any time before the conflict or during the conflict or later on in the course of the summer in its composition, did the command of the brigade, was he able to command any unit of the special purposes units?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The brigade itself, after the conflict broke out when the men had already been mobilised and when the defence lines had been established, do you know whether the brigade had the equipment and strength necessary for it to undertake any offensive action?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And to round up, Mr. Taraba, to complete this line of questioning, which tasks and assignments did the brigade have in Vitez municipality? What were its military activities from the beginning of the conflict to the end of the conflict? What was its basic function?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exclusively defence assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the brigade was the leader of the defence in the area that was under an encirclement, that is to say, at the border regions?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you make that question clearer? I'm not sure I follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Who held the lines defending this region?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The members of the Vitez Brigade. If we're talking about Vitez municipality, then it was the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What about the neighbouring municipalities, Busovaca, Novi Travnik, who held the lines there as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Novi Travnik municipality was the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade. And in Busovaca, Busovaca had its own brigade. Whether it was called the Ban Jelacic Brigade, I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So those were all municipal brigades, were they not?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let's move on now to another area. [In English] This is a short clip on video could be viewed, and I will distribute, before that, the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is it about, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It is about the late Mr. Borislav Jozic who was mentioned and is mentioned in a couple of documents and this witness, incidentally, when I was interviewing about that, and show him later on a videotape where we have that person with a certain statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Remind me who he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jozic was intelligence officer in the brigade and one who was representative, if you remember, in the commission for exchange of detained people, et cetera, nominated by the Morsink commission or Busovaca commission. So I think it is rather relevant for us, and I was looking for a person who may identify the person so that I can comment later on the substance of that interview. Your Honour, it is less than one minute, the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Has the videotape been played or exhibited before?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well, the videotape should have a number and so should the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The tape will be numbered D118/2 and the transcript D118A/2.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would require a copy for interpretation purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Actually, Your Honour, it is one question of the journalist and one answer. Indeed I am only interested in the first paragraph, but as a principle of not cutting the part, probably it would be better to see at least this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask the technicians to play the videotape.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] We are talking to Borislav Jozic and will ask him to make a statement to tell us briefly what is going on here, for he is very knowledgeable about what we are about to witness. Borislav Jozic: You know that a joint commission was set up immediately after the conflict in Vitez municipality comprising a representative of the HVO, a representative of the army of BH, delegates of the international Red Cross, delegates of UNPROFOR and representatives of the European monitors. The task of the mission was to tour the whole terrain, meaning the entire area of Vitez municipality and to record sites and locations and draw up lists of detainees or prisoners, et cetera and to have these lists exchanged at HVO and BH army levels for the purpose of exchanging prisoners. This is one of the preconditions for such an exchange to take place, or as we more aptly term it, "release" for many of these persons have neither prisoner nor detainee status. The lists have been amended, and today we are to witness the release of persons imprisoned in the school in Dubravica. You are here. You have seen that representatives are here from the International Red Cross who are in the process of registering every person along with his signature. They will be released. Their wishes are being taken into account. At the moment, some feel insecure, and their return to their native places could entail risks to their safety, their lives, et cetera. The International Red Cross is duty-bound to enable them to go to safer territory, to a place or location where they will feel secure. They are stating their wishes without the presence of third parties. The International Red Cross, therefore, is the only one who knows about them and is taking account of their wishes in creating the conditions to meet them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I have just a few questions now. Do you recognise the person in the interview?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us his name, who he is?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the late Mr. Borislav Jozic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the journalist in the clip?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What's his name, if you remember it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is Mr. Zeljo Kocaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zeljo Kocaj, was he a reporter at Vitez television station?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jozic, in the course of this interview at one point said, "Today, here in Dubravica." Did you see that interview at the time on television? Do you remember it being televised?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you happen to see it later on at any time?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether you ever had any information and when this was, that is to say, when the people detained in Dubravica school were exchanged? Do you know when that happened?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You can't give us a rough idea?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether Mr. Borislav Jozic was killed later on?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said he was the late Borislav Jozic so I do know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything regarding the circumstances of his death?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was killed by a sniper from the direction of Mahala. That was what I learnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you hear where he was killed by this sniper from the Mahala?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the exact spot, but it's difficult for me to describe where this was. It was at a crossroads. There was a kiosk selling -- a newspaper stand at the crossroads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It cannot assist us having that sort of detail. Can we move on because the witness has been giving evidence for nearly an hour already this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm just about done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Taraba, after the war when the Washington Agreements had been signed in the municipality, lists of people were made who took part in the defence of the country for the purposes of issuing certificates. We have heard testimony about that. They were certificates which the state promised to give to the participants in the war as a form of remuneration for their contribution and for the salaries that had not been paid out. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, was your name on a list of that kind?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it true that those lists contain the names of people -- let me rephrase that. Did those lists contain the names of only those people who actually took part in the war?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Why were other people's names on these lists, people who had not taken part in the war? Could you explain that to us in a few sentences, please?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It just shows the facility with which these lists were made up, because even people like my aunt, who was born in 1927, 1928, was on that list. It turned out that, in fact, she had been given a certificate which was worth more than my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What was the name of your aunt?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My aunt's name was Jozefina Taraba.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was she known by any other name?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the village they called her Filka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you saw those certificates and those shares, and she was given certificates that were worth more than those that were given to people who had a longer service time. Did you know what your aunt actually did?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My aunt, Jozefina, is 120 kilogrammes in weight and she finds it difficult to move around; she has to walk around with a walking stick.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So she, in fact, did nothing defence-wise?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more short question. Is it correct -- rather, I must rephrase that. Did you oversee the last shift that left for the front line from Vitez on the 16th of April, before the conflict, the shift that was there when the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you know, with certainty, whether there was a shift there from the Vitez Brigade on the line facing the JNA at the time that the conflict broke out in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. Taraba.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, given the witness' position on the command staff, we could ask questions about the chain of command. But we have a mountain of evidence of that already; any more would just be cumulative. So we have no questions for Captain Taraba. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We are in the position, of course, of having to do our best with the timetable, and therefore I will exclude much that I might ask witnesses like this, knowing that there are going to be other witnesses; as at present advised, the very last witness in the Cerkez defence, of whom I'm going to be able to ask many of these things. I'll try and be brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Taraba, just one thing first of all. Are you the only Vlado Taraba in Vitez, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is also a Vlado Taraba who is a late cousin of mine. He was born in 1971 or 1972. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was he doing in the conflict, if anything?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the conflict, he was on the front line in my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your village being -- have a look at this map, 2271, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just before we get there. I'm sorry to interrupt. While it's on the monitors, there's a question which I want to clear up. You were asked this question, Mr. Taraba, in leading form: "Did you oversee the last shift that left for the front line from Vitez on the 16th of April, before the conflict, the shift that was there when the conflict broke out?" It was a series of questions which I should have stopped. Now, when did you see the last shift off?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, as a rule, shifts stayed there between seven and ten days, on the line facing the army of Republika Srpska. So before the outbreak of the conflict, it was five or six days before that - I cannot say with more precision - that was when the last shift left for the line facing the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So that would be five or six days before the 16th of April; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Because the way the question was asked, it sounded as though you had seen the shift off on the 16th of April. Is your evidence that that shift was still on the front line on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, facing the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just to follow on His Honour's question. How many men were there involved on that shift on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but between 40 and 50 men. As a rule, that was the number that went to take up a shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is active members of the Viteska Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time they were shift groups or, rather, shifts from the villages which went to the front line facing the army of Republika Srpska when their turn came.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How many were in the shift? Could you give us that figure again, please?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said between 40 and 50 men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll stay with this topic, if I may. So this is not the brigade; the brigade is doing something else. This is a shift of men from the villages; do I understand you correct, Mr. Taraba?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that at that time the Vitez Brigade was only a corps. It had only the brigade command and the battalion command. And it was, as I have already said, people from the villages who went from the front line, people who only went on shifts, who were only soldiers when they were on the shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll come to the strength of the brigade maybe a little later. But what's clear, then, is that organising the village guards into shifts to go to the front line fell to you, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you are mixing up the village guards and the shift groups that went to the line facing the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Then the people who went from the villages, separate from the village guards, were organised by you, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were organised by the coordinators in those parts who cooperated with the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who were the coordinators, then, please?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The coordinators were men who coordinated the departure of shifts to the line facing the army of Republika Srpska, and the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's clear enough. But who were they, these coordinators? They were members of the brigade, were they?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to tell you their names?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want to know if the coordinators were members of the brigade. Simple question.

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. So that we have the command structure, and you've been asked about command structures in general by Mr. Kovacic, so that we have the command structure for those going to the front line, they are people in the villages who are willing and able to go to the front line, and they are coordinated in that activity by brigade members called coordinators.

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you, in respect of the last mission to the front line, coordinated the activity overall.

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received lists of men in the shift that were to go to the front line facing the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's have another look at this document just so that we can be quite sure what you're saying about it. Document 653 again, I'm afraid. It's a very simple document in that it's headed "The Viteska Brigade"; it's said to be the 1st Battalion of the Vitez Information and Security Service; it's dated the 14th of April, 1993, so it's before the conflict; it's said to be a list of personnel from the 1st Battalion of the Viteska Brigade per village of either deployment or something like that, and then it lists them, the 1st Company and the soldiers. These were men in those villages available to the Viteska Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a list of men who, at a given moment, in case of need, could be mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's go back here just for a couple of minutes to 1992. We'll leave that document where it is for now, if that's all right. Thank you very much, indeed. In 1992 the Tomasevic Brigade had two battalions, and the second one related to Vitez; are we correct about that?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Cerkez was the commander of the 2nd Battalion at some stage; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, what was his role, then?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mario Cerkez was in the brigade command of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade, and if I recall rightly, I think he was the chief of the brigade, with its seat in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he have any special interest in Vitez, the town from which he came, and so on? Did he?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you should ask him that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was he also the commander of the municipal armed forces of the HVO in Vitez, by that title, in 1992, please?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Vitez there were no municipal armed forces. But in late May and early June, a municipal staff of the HVO was established which, at a given moment, was the successor of the former municipal staff of the Territorial Defence. This is a civilian organisation, so to say, which organised shifts going to Galica, Vlasic. And later on --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll take that elsewhere probably with another witness. Just confirm this for me, please. The soldiers who were members of the 2nd Battalion of the Tomasevic Brigade, by and large, came from Vitez, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that we cannot talk about soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, what about the people who paraded at the oath-taking ceremony in the summer of 1992? Were they soldiers or were they elderly reservists, which is it? They were soldiers, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what time you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The summer of 1992, August, I think, in the stadium at Vitez. Don't you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't, because I am not a member of the HDZ so I tried, as far as was possible, to keep myself apart from any activities taking place at that time because I was a member of the former political party of the former Yugoslavia and certain individuals looked at me with -- looked at me down their noses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do I understand your evidence then to be this: That the non-soldiers, or whatever they were, of the 2nd Battalion of the Tomasevic Brigade simply became the same sort of creature, a non-soldier of the 1st Battalion of the Viteska Brigade when it was formed; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When the Viteska Brigade was formed, its first battalion was made of the same human assets that had existed in the 2nd Battalion of the Tomasevic Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the command which used to be part of the 2nd Battalion of Stjepan Tomasevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Only the command. I see. So if I was to suggest to you, let's go back to this document, please, if I was to suggest to you, take any one of these villages, that the soldiers shown there might have been similarly working for the Tomasevic Brigade's 2nd Battalion in 1992, would you accept that or reject that or do you say "I don't know." Which is it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say they were not soldiers of the 2nd Battalion of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade but that they were people who went on shifts facing the line of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's move on. You've spoken about the number of days it required to prepare people, for example, to go to the front line. Do you remember that passage of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I just want to -- just before I forget it, your cousin, Vlado Taraba, went to the front line with that last mission, did he, a few days before?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know, but I think he didn't. Are you referring to the line facing the army of Republika Srpska that was there during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. It may be my mistake in understanding your answer. You tell us, please, where your cousin, Vlado Taraba, was in the course of this conflict starting on the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in the village, in his village, or rather my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll come to your village in a minute as I was going to do some questions ago. But before we move on to that, no brigade existed, is that right, until after the conflict started. That's your evidence, is it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there was only a brigade nucleus, the command of the brigade and the command of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps you'd like to look at this document, please, it's 636.1. It's not very clear in the original, but you'll have that. English for the ELMO, thank you very much. Now, this is a document, comes from Mr. Cerkez dated the 10th of April 1993 before the conflict elements of extract for the mobilisation plan and it says this: "Pursuant to the conclusions of the seminar for chiefs of organisation and personnel and in conjunction with the extract from the basic mobilisation plan, we are sending you the necessary elements for the Vitez Brigade which is classed as an "R" infantry brigade, according to the temporary establishment number which is given." And then the brigade is set out with a number of soldiers, 2.841, front, various other things including the assembly point and a first degree of readiness, said to be six hours. Now, how would you explain that document to us, please? You are really the theoretician?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never seen this document before in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, you are a theoretician. You taught the subject. You should be able to help us. Can you help us, please.

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a subject matter which was never taught according to the curriculum I went through. We were talking about mobilisation in general and the types of mobilisation there were partial, public, secret and so on, but we never discussed these details and I have to admit that this is my weak point because I never did this kind of work in practice. I only taught in schools.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well, I'll take the document back, thank you. Let's look at exactly where you live and we can sort that out and where your cousin was. Does this map, take your time and look at it if you are able to understand a map, does it show where you lived? The usher will give you a pointer and you can point it out on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's your home there. On the road off from the main westerly road and just up in the direction of -- that's Bila and that road leads off, eventually, I've forgotten now but -- very well. And that's where you were on the night of the 15th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That is my house where my parents live and where I lived most -- for a good part of my life, but I was actually in my flat in Vitez in the building opposite the health centre, if that means anything to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It probably does, but we'll have to deal with it just by the map. Let's have the map here, please. This is D88/2. Your flat is in Vitez in the centre, yes?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And so when you were summoned on that night by Ivan Budimir from your village you, in fact, didn't go to your village, you went somewhere else; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that would involve your going to the right of the map. It's a long time ago. Can you remember what route you took or did you just drive in the most obvious way down to Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only by the most obvious way to Rijeka. I took the road to Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you say that you didn't see anything unusual. What time was it that you went down to Rijeka, please?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was about midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Did your route take you by the brigade's headquarters or not or don't you remember?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Past the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. You can't say one way or another what was going on inside the brigade's command, can you?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. It would, in any event, have armed soldiers at its doors, I imagine; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The brigade's headquarters in the centre of Vitez, the cinema complex.

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. You got to Rijeka and it was down there in Rijeka, it's just off the map as shown on the -- or it's on the map as shown on the screen, that you were given your instructions for the evening; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any specific instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want to know who was meeting, please, at the Sumarija in Rijeka? Who was meeting there?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were members of the command of the 2nd Battalion of the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The 2nd Battalion of the Vitez Brigade already existed then, did it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I mean the 1st Battalion. I meant the 1st Battalion of the Vitez Brigade because that was the only battalion and it was the command of the Vitez Brigade. I am talking about the command of the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was your terms to choose the 2nd Battalion, was that just a slip of the tongue, Mr. Taraba?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was. It was a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, the command of the 1st Battalion of the Viteska Brigade, who was that? How many people? Give us the names.

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember there was Mr. Bertovic, Mr. Grabovac, there was Mr. Milicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just the three of them?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, there were other people but I can't remember now. I can't say who was present with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is that Karlo Grabovac?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. But this is just the command, because at this time, you had what position in the brigade? What was your proper position or rank?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have a rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was your position in the command, please?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the assistant commander for operative and training jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Having been appointed by who to that job?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was appointed by Mr. Bertovic at the beginning of December 1992 while the battalion was still part of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So roughly how many members of this nucleus were there there on that night? Give us an idea.

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, I think there were six or seven men. I can't remember exactly, because it's been a long time. I didn't think it was important.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So it was quite an informal meeting, in a way presided over by Bertovic.

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that it was the practice in such situations to call the members of the command if any movements had been observed, if there was reason to call together the command, so it was the thousand and first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's not an answer to my question, Mr. Taraba. The question was quite simple: Quite an informal meeting presided over by Bertovic; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have any formal meeting. We were just told that certain movements had been observed and that's where it ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Bertovic had got his instructions from whom, his boss, Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the military chain of command, it should have been Mr. Cerkez, but I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you telling the Chamber on this day that there was simply a generalised warning that needed some sort of attention? Is that what Bertovic told you?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to come back to that meeting in due course. I don't know whether the Chamber wants to break now or later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Probably now is as convenient as any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now. Mr. Taraba, would you be back in half an hour at half past eleven.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Taraba, a little more assistance, please, with what happened that night. The meeting you'd had with the command ended at what time?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the conventional terms, there was no meeting. I believe I have already mentioned that it was around half past eleven, 12.00, that I was in the command, and when I entered Mr. Bertovic told me what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We know there were no soldiers of the brigade to call on because there was no brigade at that time. So what did you do to satisfy Mr. Bertovic's orders?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have said yourself, there were no soldiers. And no specific assignments were given me by Mr. Bertovic, as far as I was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to the other people there, what did they do to try and satisfy his concerns or Cerkez's concerns? What did they do?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, did they do anything, or did they do nothing?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came around 12.00, I was told what had been done or, rather, why I had been called to the command, and practically until the morning I did nothing. There were members of the command, and it was the common practice in a situation like that, when members of the command are all together under some emergency conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're not giving a picture -- it's entirely my fault, I know. I simply don't understand what you're saying happened. Let's take it in stages. So far as you understand it, Mr. Taraba, nothing had happened by the time that you arrived at half past eleven or 12.00; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question? I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nothing had happened, by which I mean no troops had been deployed by the time you arrived at half past eleven or 12.00.

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know. I did not ask the commander, nor did he say anything to that effect to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think you told us something about some troops going off to do something in relation to Vranjska or Kruscica. What did troops do to go and protect Vranjska and Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander told me that the groups which used to go to the front line against the army of Republika Srpska, that their attention had been drawn to raise the alert, to be more watchful and report to the command about anything they might observe; and in case of an attack, to take up the fight, that is, protect that part, that is, those places, their village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. So the commander had spoken to the local village coordinators, had he? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I -- that is my guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, then, we better go back once more to 653, please, if the usher would be so good. How many soldiers do you say were involved in doing this watchful process?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that they are not soldiers now. They would be soldiers for those seven or ten days while on a shift in the defence. Now they are the villagers of a village who live in a village and go about their daily business.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, here are the soldiers. Now, we can't see the number of -- sorry, not the soldiers, the whatever they are. Here are the men. We can't see the number in Rijeka because it happens to be illegible. But apart from Rijeka, are there any other places - have a look at the list, please - with resident men who are going to be able to look after either Kruscica or Vranjska? Are there any other places there marked which have got soldiers or non-soldiers who are going to be able to look after Kruscica or Vranjska?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These localities -- it needs to be said that Kruscica is not inhabited by Muslims alone; a part of Kruscica is also inhabited by Croats, which means that by and large, from these localities which gravitate to the villages of Kruscica and Vranjska, that it is these men who are engaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They're not listed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, if we're getting no where with this witness -- I mean, it should be made plain, Mr. Kovacic, if we don't understand what the witness is saying, then his evidence is virtually worthless, and there are occasions when it's very difficult to follow what's being said. But let us go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will. I've been trying to get a picture from this witness, and I've only got a couple more questions to ask about the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It comes to this, Mr. Taraba: You were under the stairs, I think, at some other stage during the night --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It was during the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it in the day?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, in the early hours in the morning, leading up to 5.00, 6.00, were you still in the Sumarija building?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, then, if we look at the map. It's gone again. Here it is. Just remind the Chamber, you were there in the building and if we look just -- that's perfect. We can see on the right a feature called Hrasno, yes? You know that feature?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's only a few kilometres away from your area. Did you hear artillery firing from there, please, early in the morning?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would you -- do you say you would have heard artillery firing from Hrasno when you were in Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is some four or five kilometres away from Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were a soldier, you would have heard it, wouldn't you, if there was artillery?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I became a soldier because of the circumstances. I am not a professional soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Look, please, at this document, 676. In the course of the night, please, when you say you were at the headquarters in Rijeka, did you receive any other instructions from your commander or from anyone else? Just yes or no to that question and then we'll look at the document. Did you receive any other instructions, any update of any instructions in the course of the night?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see if we look at this document that you have in front of you, if we could just see a tiny bit up, this is a document that apparently was drawn -- it was drawn on the 16th of April at 1.30 in the morning and it goes to the commander of the HVO brigade, Mr. Cerkez, and to PPN units. And it says this: It's a combat command to prevent activity and blockade the broader territory of Kruscica, Vranjska, and Donja Veceriska and it says quite specifically, "On the basis of command and assessment, we expect enemy attack in the direction of Kruscica." I'm not going to read it all, the Judges have seen it before, but it comes after your 11.30 meeting and it is quite specific as to preparedness for attack at 5.30. Are you saying you knew nothing of this, of this order? You know nothing of this order?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because on your evidence, and I'm going to probably part with this question from this topic, on your evidence, there was no Viteska Brigade apart from the headquarters staff of five or six people in the building where you were; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Therefore, a combat command like this could operate only on those five or six people because there were no soldiers; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This command was received by the commander so that I have never seen this order. This is the first time I set my eyes on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. I'm going to move on very rapidly and spend very little time with this witness from now on. I've got a couple of topics. Topic number one arises from this: When did you leave this area and go back to your mother's or your father's house? How many days later?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five or six days after the beginning of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So then you are out to the west of Vitez and you don't spend any time in the centre of Vitez; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And your cousin, the other Vlado Taraba, was with you in that same village area; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And your cousin had no command or superior position in the Vitez Brigade in the way that you did; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, what position of command did he ever have?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not have any position in the command. He was a local villager.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And as I said, when the need arose, he went to the front line against the Republika Srpska army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, in Rijeka then, it might have been possible to find you, but it wouldn't have been possible to find the other Vlado Taraba, would it, because he was in his own home village, and you were at least in Rijeka for four or five, or five or six days; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In Rijeka, there's a house belonging to somebody called Asim Sivro, remember?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Mr. Sivro, but I do not know where his house is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You know a man named Zoran Rajic, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Zoran Rajic is a fairly forceful man, is he?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean his build?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, by personality, is he a forceful man?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know him enough to say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, didn't the two of you go to Asim Sivro's house in Rijeka where there was a young boy whose father was in Kruscica, and didn't you - or more probably the other man, Rajic, judging by your personality, the other man, Rajic - didn't one or other of you to tell that boy to tell his father to surrender in Kruscica otherwise his throat would be cut? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you remember any incident like that happening in the house of Sivro, and as a way of trying to get Sivro in Kruscica to surrender? Do you remember any such incident, please, Mr. Taraba, and tell us about it, please, if you do?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your job in the brigade included the drafting and typing of letters, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do you mean, letters? Letters regarding the army, if there is an organisation, such as command, then letters are a very rare phenomenon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have a look at this document please, 1143.2. I'm going to go to the last of a sequence of three documents first because I just want to confirm something with you. The 2nd Battalion of which you became an officer was commanded by Zarko Saric, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, following the establishment of the 2nd Battalion sometime after July or August.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, that's all I want. Look at this document and don't bother yourself at all with the contents for the time being. It's dated the 12th of July, and if we look at the bottom immediately above the distribution list there's "VT/ZS" -- sorry, my mistake. I misled. Don't worry, the right document is coming your way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Ms. Kind was entitled to think I was going chronologically and I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you look at this document when it comes to you, at the bottom, above the distribution list, we see "VT/ZS," and we see it's over the name of Zarko Saric. "VT" stands for you, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are my initials, "VT," but I do not know whether, indeed, they are my initials in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, if it's been suggested elsewhere that you drafted this document, would you accept that as a probability?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a probability I may have, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's have a look at the two documents that precede it, and we'll start with 1139.2, which you already have. Now, I'll just read you the contents of this in English on the ELMO. This is from Cerkez, on the 6th of July, and it relates to the death of Colonel Duncan's interpreter. That's something that happened very near to the headquarters of the 2nd Battalion, so you must remember that. Do you remember the shooting of the interpreter?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I do remember, and that, if my memory serves me well, it was a lady who worked as an interpreter but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. The body of the letter says: "I shall personally do everything possible - and this I promise you - to find the perpetrator, should he be from the ranks of the HVO. I am truly sorry about the death ..." and it goes on. Was it believed at the time that the killer of this interpreter was within the ranks of the HVO, please, Mr. Taraba?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was an assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's go to the next document, which is 1141.3. Now, this is a document that comes, simply, three days later, following the expressions of condolence to Colonel Duncan, and it's an instruction by Mario Cerkez to the commanders of the four battalions and the commander of the independent unit, and it says -- it's a warning and it says: "1. All housing facilities used by UNPROFOR will be identified by the United Nations flag. 2. HVO members are not allowed to ... do anything ... detrimental to the ... housing ... 3. Make this known to all units and all commanders ranging from squad commanders ... 4. Commanders ... are personally responsible to me for making this warning efficacious." And then if we go from that document to your document, which comes again three days later, the one drafted by you, we see your document is effectively the same document now signed by Zarko Saric. So I have simply two questions to ask you: Was the document that you, it may be, drafted of the 12th of July a reflection of the killing near to your headquarters of that interpreter, please?
