utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was still believed, was it, by the 12th of July that a member of the HVO may have been responsible for that murder?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there, to your knowledge, any investigation by Cerkez or, indeed, even by your commander, Saric, of the circumstances of that death?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that an investigation was ordered to go into the circumstances of this murder, but I do not know what the results of the investigation were because that was not my business.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. But you would accept, of course, that both Saric and Cerkez had a duty to investigate and a duty to instigate process and punishment of any offender; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should think so. And the order shows that there is an order to conduct an investigation. But there are people who do these things, and that was not part of my responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not sure it does show that. You remember an order for an investigation; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, as far as I can remember, an order was issued to conduct the investigation and identify a possible perpetrator, possibly of the HVO, who had fired those shots, that is, who had committed that murder. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course, no one was ever detained, arrested, or punished, was he?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are authorities which did that, and you should ask that of them because it was their responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mosunj was the area where there was the quarry; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It had heavy artillery in it that the HVO used; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the heavy artillery moved about. But they were outside the Vitez Brigade, and I do not know where they were positioned or what their orders were. They did not make it part of our formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may have moved about, but it was based sometimes in the Mosunj quarry; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, if my memory serves me well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And sometimes it fired from the Mosunj quarry.

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I guess so, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, you were there. It's only a couple hundred metres away. You must be able to remember if the artillery in the quarry was sometimes fired; it makes a very big bang. It was fired from there, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think also - I'm grateful to Mr. Lopez-Terres - it was in that same quarry that quite a number of the trucks of the Convoy of Joy were looted in June of 1993; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VLADO TARABA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about it from journalists who were in my house. But at that time, I was at the front line, that day I was at the front line. Just to explain it to you. During the war there were BBC journalists in my house, and it was from them that I learned about the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness, it seems to me, can't know anything about the truth or accuracy of what Borislav Jozic was saying on the clip, so I'm not going to ask about that, and I'm not going to go through the process of dealing with his aunt being listed. The Chamber will recollect that when we're dealing with a listing of people on those lists, there's always another document that deals with wounding and something of that sort. It doesn't apply to the aunt, I don't think. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We have no questions for redirect, Your Honour. I'm sorry, it wasn't recorded. We have no questions on redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I heard it. Mr. Taraba, thank you for coming to the International Tribunal. That concludes your evidence. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll deal with it appropriately. Yes, have the next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Zuljevic.

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On behalf of the Cerkez Defence, I shall be questioning you and I should like to ask you to answer my questions nice and slowly to give the interpreters a chance to do their work. For the record, could you please state your name and surname, your date and place of birth?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Fabijan Zuljevic. I was born on the 14th of February, 1961, in the village of Krcevine, Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zuljevic, you are married and the father of two children ages 10 and 12; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What education have you had?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I went to a vocational school. I am a chemist or chemistry technician and plastics technician.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you serve in the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where and when, please?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: In 1980, in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you obtain a military rank of any kind?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What are you doing now, Mr. Zuljevic?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I am a member of the army of the federation at present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what rank do you hold?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I am a sergeant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Before the war, you worked in Sintevit, did you not?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Slobodan Princip Seljo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Up until what year?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I worked there until 19 -- from 1981 to 1991, and I was put on standby after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Why were you put on standby?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was no more work to do in the plant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zuljevic, do you remember who was the director of Sintevit at the time?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember, it was Mr. Alija Basic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Alija Basic belongs to what ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: He is a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who was the shop steward in the company you worked for?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: We had Croats and Muslims. There was Munir Varupa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Varupa is also a Muslim, is he not?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At that time, when you said that there was not too much work, was there any national discrimination with respect to putting workers on standby?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was the national composition, roughly speaking, in your firm?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, half/half.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zuljevic, you said that you were in the village of Donja Dubravica, and that is a village that many people refer to as Krizancevo Selo?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I live in Donja Dubravica, that is to say, the hamlet of Krizancevo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask the usher to place on the ELMO Z2271, which is the map that we've already used quite a few times, for the witness to be able to refer to the map and point out the relevant localities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zuljevic, for us to better understand where you lived, show us where your house was, looking at the map on your right-hand side. Take a look at the map, you'll find it easier and point your house out to us, please.

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said at the beginning, that in 1991, you were left without a job. What did you do?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I stayed at home, and the unfortunate events started, the wars. And when the attack on Bosnia-Herzegovina began, I reported to the crisis command because I considered it my civil duty to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Let us take it one-by-one, step-by-step. You said that there was an attack launched by the JNA on Bosnia-Herzegovina and as a citizen you felt duty-bound to report to the authorities for defence purposes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you went to the Crisis Staff, where was the Crisis Staff located?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff was, how shall I explain this, well, it was in Vitez. It was where -- by Marijan Skopljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan Skopljak was the head of that Crisis Staff, was he?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you reported to him, did you?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, not to him, but there was a coordinator there representing our village, in charge of our village, and it was with this Skopljak -- well, actually we reported to that other man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Mr. Zuljevic, the Crisis Staff headed by Mr. Marijan Skopljak, was it also called the municipal staff of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Mr. Zuljevic, when did you report at the staff and Mr. Skopljak to go to the front line, what -- when was that?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was the autumn, perhaps November or December.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Of which year?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: 1991 moving into 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was it like? How were -- how was this organised? How did people go to do their shifts, go on shift?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the shifts against the Serbs, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: The village organised this. We had a sort of coordinator there, and it was his job , he was in charge of the shifts. And he would put us in these shifts and told us, in the village, that we would have to prepare ourselves to go on shift, and 50 to 60 people would go to do their -- these shifts facing the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At that time, could you tell us where you personally went when you were on shift?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was at Slatka Vode. Turbe, I was there once, and we went towards Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Mr. Zuljevic, how were you transferred to -- how did you go to the defence line from your village? How did you get there?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the late Slavko Papic told us where to go, where we were to assemble, the collecting point, and then we would go in a van, a minibus or van, whatever you'd like to call it. Mostly they were vans, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. How long did you stay in a shift?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, shifts lasted up to seven days, a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How many people from your village took part in those shifts?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Up to 19 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And how many men in the village, as far as you know, were military-able men? How many at that time?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: There were about 35 to 40 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That would make it half. Half of them took part in the shifts, the other half did not; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you returned from the shift, what did you do then in your home, in your house?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, when I came back home, I went about my daily business.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And when you were up at the defence lines, did you have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who gave you those weapons?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, from Slimena, and some people from the Territorial Defence that had taken it over from the former JNA so that the weapons were up there at the defence line. We would come to the defence lines without weapons, then we would be given weapons by the people who were already up there at the defence line. So one shift would hand over their weapons to the shift that would replace them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Mr. Zuljevic, you mentioned that you went to the defence lines in vans or minibuses. What route did you take? How did you get to your shift?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: We went towards Novi Travnik and up above Novi Travnik through a Muslim settlement. I think its name is Kalinska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where is Kalinska Street, Mr. Zuljevic?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Kalinska belongs to Novi Travnik and it is up above the town and on the way to the defence line, thereabouts. I don't know how else to describe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That part of town where Kalinska Street lies, you said was predominantly inhabited by Muslims; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In Kalinska Street, was there a checkpoint of any kind?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a checkpoint. And when we passed by that way up to Slatka Vode there was an incident that occurred not in the sense of shooting, but there was some provocation and the police would come to intervene. And so for a time, we were given a police escort along that route.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who caused the incidents that you've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Probably the members of the BH army because they already had some of their people there. I don't know whether this was leading up to a war of any kind, but they were -- or whether they were just provocations, but that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The people who stopped you at the checkpoint in Kalinska Street, and you said that they were members of the BiH army, did they know where you were going?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How -- what was their treatment towards you when they stopped you? What was their conduct? What would they do?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, they would insult us, call us detrimental names. But we didn't respond to that. We had no weapons. We had nothing at all. So we were told that if we had to pass checkpoints of this kind that the police should be called in and -- but there was no police escort to begin with, so that's what happened, incidents of this kind took place. But there was no shooting or firing of any kind. They were just insults, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Mr. Zuljevic, on occasion, because of the prevailing circumstances, did you have to take a byroad to arrive at your shift point?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, sometimes we went towards Stari Travnik, and we went on foot via towards the village of Prica. That happened twice, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At these defence lines that you went to, were there members of the Muslim ethnicity, and did they have their assignments as well?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was there any cooperation between you and them at the defence lines?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, my particular defence line was not able to communicate with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that the shifts would last between seven and ten days and that you would return to the village after that?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At that time, and we are talking about the end of 1992 and later on, the beginning of 1993, were there any village guards organised in your particular village?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were. They were organised, but they were organised to defend the village, and I'm talking about Krizancevo Selo, Dubravica. Up above us there were some Serbs, so this was protection against them and against some local criminals who were rampant. There was a lot of looting of cars so we wanted to protect our village from that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Do you remember who the commander of the village guard in your village was?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: The commander -- well, actually he wasn't a commander, he was just elected by the villagers, but his name was Zdravko Kozina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you said that the villagers elected him, chose him, was this any formal type of voting or how did you choose him? How did he become a commander? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No, he was a young man. He had been to university, and he had some -- lists and papers of some kind, and so he chose people who could go around the village and do night patrols, but there was no election of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Zuljevic, who organised the village guard in your village?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: The villagers themselves did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you ever take part in the village guards and were on shift there?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We cooperated together with the Muslims, and the Muslims would patrol together with us. It was a joint village guard. It was not one group, one ethnicity, or another. We did this together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, the people from your village, you said there were about 19 of them who went to do shifts at Slatka Vode, were they all members of the village guard when they were not doing their shift?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, some were; some were not. Some said they didn't want to take part in the village guards, because they said, "Well, when we're off up at the defence line facing the Serbs, you're at home sleeping." So some of them didn't want to do this type of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What kind of weaponry did you have in the village guards when you were on duty?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, mostly hunting rifles, and perhaps a rifle here or there, if somebody had sold a cow and been able to buy a rifle. But otherwise they were double-barrelled guns, whatever they're called.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were there enough weapons to go around to all members of the village guards?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you hand over weapons in the village guards as you did in the shifts, what you told us a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: According to the best of your recollection, Mr. Zuljevic, were there any changes in the composition of the village guards? You said that they were of mixed composition to begin with. Did that ever change?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it did change after some incidents took place; like the one in Kruscica, for example, where the police of the BH army met our police and beat up some policemen. A cousin of mine, Vlatko Zuljevic, he was a 16-year-old boy, they almost killed him. So there were incidents of this kind and tension, tense situations, and we couldn't trust each other any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now that you've mentioned Kruscica, Mr. Zuljevic, let me ask you this: Do you know whether in Kruscica, at any given locality, people would rally when they had to go to do shifts?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a hunting lodge in Kruscica, that's how we referred to it, as a hunting lodge, and they would gather there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know that place personally? Have you been there?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you ever go there and gather there to go off and do your shift?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where is that lodge located in Kruscica, if you look at it from your village?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's part of the village, actually. There's a river and it's across the river. About 100 metres on the other bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you have a uniform of any kind, Mr. Zuljevic?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The lodge you were talking about, was it also called the Motel or Hotel Lovac?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zuljevic, throughout the time we are talking about, until the conflict broke out on the 16th of April, did you go to do shifts at Slatka Vode?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember your last shift at Slatka Vode?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I remember. The last shift was before the conflict in Ahmici, that last shift where I personally was the shift commander. I stayed there for five days or six; five, I think. On the 16th, a reconnaissance man came from Novi Travnik to tell me that there was war in Vitez; that he was on his way to tell everyone from Novi Travnik about it. There was a shift at Mravinac from Novi Travnik; it was supposed to be there but it couldn't come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. So that was on the 16th of April. Do you remember what time it was?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was about 1300 or 1400 hours. About 1400 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Zuljevic, how long you had been there before the 16th of April? When did you leave for that shift?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I think it was about five days. I can't tell you the exact date I left for that shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You say you were the commander of that part of the shift that came from your village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In your estimate, how many men from Vitez and its environs were there?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: About 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What did you do when you were told by this reconnaissance man who came from Novi Travnik that a war had broken out in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I went with Mr. Stipo Cerkez. First, I told my men that if I didn't come back from Vilenica, they should continue in the direction of Bugojno and Novi Travnik. I went around Vilenica looking for a way to get out, because I had no communication with my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did you try to establish communication with the command in Vitez to learn what was going on?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you succeed in that?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you have any means of communication?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No. Except there was a relay -- a transmitter where I tried. It probably belonged to Travnik, Novi Travnik. I don't know what unit that was. And I tried but I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So what decision did you make?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I went back in the evening, at about 11.00, and I decided to retreat, withdraw, at about 4.00 because there was no one at Vilenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you decided to withdraw from the line, and to go where?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. What happened to the equipment you were issued with at the front line?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I took what was necessary, I took it with me. I left behind the kitchen, a military vehicle, which we couldn't take to Kalinska. So that was left behind at the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were any weapons left behind?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. We took the weapons and the ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What route did you take in the direction of home, of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, from Slatka Vode I went via Vilenica, where I arrived at the transmitter on Vilenica, and from there I went toward the Stojkovici base.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. Where is this Stojkovici base, exactly?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the Stojkovici base is below Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. In the municipality of Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Zuljevic, what the members of the shifts from Novi Travnik did when they learned that a conflict had broken out in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When did you arrive in Stojkovici? What day was it?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: It was the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What did you do then?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: There, I established contact with my commander, Anto Bertovic, and I asked about the situation. He said it was terrible. There was a war; there were refugees from Poculica, there were some men from there. He said I should wait there in the base and he would come and fetch us, that a minibus and two vans would come and fetch us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did that happen?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In that conversation, did Mr. Bertovic tell you anything about mobilisation being proclaimed?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When he told you that there was an armed conflict, how did you feel at that moment?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I felt terrible. I didn't even know where I was. The phones were ringing -- they were working, so I called home to find out what had happened to my wife and children. My wife answered and said that my cousin had been killed and that my brother had been seriously wounded. You can only imagine how a man would feel in such a situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that vehicles came to fetch you. Where did they take you?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the vehicles came and took us to the primary school in Bila, in Stara Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: And then we got out of the vehicles, because we didn't dare go further because of Grbavica. Then I contacted Bertovic again, and he told me that he would let us know what to do next. And then he called me again and said that we should disband the army from Mosunj -- well, not the army but the people who were there on the line. And the rest set out with me in a bus which was driven by Ivica -- I can't recall the last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Don't worry about these details. So, in short, Bertovic said that the men who had come with you from the Slatka Vode position, where they had been on shifts, should be allowed to go home.

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The people went home; some by bus, some on foot, and some in other ways; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you went to your village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said awhile ago that men had been in your shift from various villages. Would you repeat the names of the villages, for the record?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The people were from Zaselje, Veceriska, Nadioci, Santici, Krizancevo Selo, and Krcevine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. Then you were told by your wife over the telephone, and then you came home. What did you find when you arrived at home?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I found my family. When I came home, my wife and children were there, and I stayed there for two days. Because my house is near the Muslim village of Nadioci, so I stayed at home for another two days, for my own security and because of my children and my wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you came home in the evening of the 17th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At that time, were there any armed conflicts? Was there any fighting near your house?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No real fighting, but there were provocations in the direction of the school. But not in the very spot where my house is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did your wife tell you more about how and where your relatives had been killed?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: She told me that my cousin had been killed in Nadioci, in a wood. He was killed by Muslims, but I don't know any more about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said, Mr. Zuljevic, that you stayed at home for two days; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. At that time when you arrived, had a defence line already been established in your village?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, beside my house, between Novaci and me, there was not a line, but everyone sat in front of his own house, elderly men, younger men. And others had organised in the direction of Tolovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What did you do then? Did you join your fellow villagers?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where, at that time, were the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: The Muslim forces, when I was at home, were in Novaci, which is why I stayed at home for two days. But then they went toward Mahala, and then I left in the direction of Lazine, that is, Tolovici, where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. Would you be kind enough, Mr. Zuljevic, to show us on the map where Novaci is in relation to your village.

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Approximately, elevation 437 -- well, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So a little bit above elevation 437.

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Approximately there. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that the Muslim forces withdrew from Novaci.

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where did they go?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: They went toward Mahala. That's toward the town, up there in the town, and they stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It was then, in fact, that this Muslim village which is immediately next to yours remained empty,?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Immediately next to our village, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. So the front line of defence, which consisted of everybody sitting in front of his house and protecting it, now became unnecessary; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where did you set up a defence line after that?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were no defence lines after that. But I went toward Lazine where there was a line, toward Tolovici. That's above Krizancevo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Would you please show that on the map. Where is Lazine?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Elevation 536, it's here. Here. So elevation 536, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And when you arrived there, had a defence line already been established?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, no. It was a training ground belonging to the former JNA where people came from Zenica to train, but it wasn't much. There wasn't a real defence line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What day was it when you turned up at Lazine?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: It was the 19th or the 20th. I think it was the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned in the introduction that Zdravko Kozina was the commander of the village guard, did he have the same function at Lazine?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did anyone representing the Vitez Brigade come to Lazine to issue orders or instructions?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The commander, Zdravko Kozina, as far as you could remember, did he have any contacts with the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: There was no Vitez Brigade then. Of course he had contacts because he had to go and get instructions about what to do and how.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that at that time, you were not aware of the Vitez Brigade. You said that there was no Vitez Brigade at the time.

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When, to the best of your recollection, did your unit at Lazine join the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: It was in 1993, maybe it was April or May we went to Slatka Vode. We had pictures, later on we were given some kind of identity cards in 1993. I can't remember exactly whether it was, April or May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to show us on the map the position where you were at Lazine and the position at which the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I have just shown it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On the map please, not on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we were here at elevation 536 and the army was right above us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, I would like to ask the usher to help. Yes, it's okay. So you were somewhere by elevation 536. Where was the army of BH?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Here, where this black line was. Here, in front of Tolovici that is, about 100 metres from us. Between these two roads here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So Tolovici was held by the army of B and H?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: To the left of you, we see the village of Krcevine. Who held it?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: The villagers of Krcevine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. Who held the Grabak location at the top of the monitor?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was held by the Muslims. It was a Serb village but the Serbs moved away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: To the right of Tolovici, we see Poculica?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who controlled Poculica at that time?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: The Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Below that, we see Vrhovine. Who controlled Vrhovine?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: The Muslims. That was one ethnic place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Zuljevic, what sort of weapons did you have at the front line?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: We had infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you have any kind of heavy weapons? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No. Except for an anti-aircraft machine-gun which was left behind by the Serbs when they retreated from Tolovici. They went to Teslic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell us, what kind of weapons did the army of B and H have at the positions you described?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, here above Grabak, let me show you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: They had an anti-aircraft machine-gun and a three-barrelled gun and later on when the general attacks took place on Vitez, they had a tank. There was another tank at Grabak, in the direction of Krcevine, they attacked Krcevine. There was a third tank in the village of Poculica, and a fourth tank in Zabljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned all these weapons. Were they all used in the attack on your line?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When was it used?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was towards the end in 1993. It could have been used in October, November.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. And that position that you have just described to us, did you manage to fortify yourselves, to dig trenches and shelters?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And during the conflict, were you at any time ordered to launch an offensive action, to leave the trenches and move forward to the positions that you told us about?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Which was your principal task at that front line?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Why the defence of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Until the end of the war against the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registry please show Z70.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I should also like to ask you to turn to page 15. Mr. Zuljevic, will you please look at number 79. Under 79, it says Zuljevic (Drago) Fabijan, born on the 14th of February 1961; is that you?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Will you now look at the signatures? This is the last column on the right. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: It is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So these particulars are yours, but this is not your signature, is it?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We do not need this exhibit anymore. To the best of your recollection and your experience, when did you join the organised -- that is, armed resistance against the JNA attacks on Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was when there was this municipal staff, that is when I joined. This was recognised as of the 16th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And were you issued some certificates for that?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was because of the certificates and the recognition of the service, but mostly because of the certificates [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps have the certificates with you, I don't mean here but at home?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you use them for anything?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. They are practically worthless.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned in your -- in the introduction that you used to work in the SPS compound. Did you ever meet Mario Cerkez there?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Why, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But he did not work for the same company as you did.

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No, but we were both at the SPS Slobodan Princip, but our workplaces were different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what was your -- how did Mario Cerkez strike you as a fellow worker?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: As a fellow worker and a citizen, I thought well of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear or see him manifest any aggression, attack, or verbal abuse against Muslims or express himself pejoratively about anybody else?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, and he even had friends, I mean Mario Cerkez -- Mario Cerkez, but there was no Croat who did not have a Muslim friend so that we worked together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Zuljevic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Kordic's Defence does not have any questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It might be more convenient to deal with it after the luncheon adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It would be entirely as Your Honour pleases, unless I could simply ask the witness one question so that I can tidy something up over lunch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The name of his cousin who he says was killed at Nadioci and then I can deal with that

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could you just tell us the name of your cousin who you say was killed on the day of the 16th?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Not the 16th. Before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. His name?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Vlatko Zuljevic. No, sorry, on the 16th, it was another relative, Ivan Zuljevic who was killed then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Zuljevic, that is the time for us to adjourn. Could you remember not to speak to anyone about your evidence during the adjournment, and that includes members of the Defence team, until it's over. Could you be back, please, at half past two. If you'd like to go now, there's something -- it's nothing to do with your evidence, there's something I want to deal with briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.01 p.m. 21 22 23 24 25 1

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you joined up the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade, you joined up as a soldier, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you stayed a soldier from that moment on, right up until the end of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All that happened was that whereas to begin with you were in the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade, there came a time when you changed from that brigade and were in a brigade that had a different title, that's all.

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I was a member of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade. The Vitez Brigade didn't exist at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exactly. But in due course, as a member of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade, you changed over and you became a member of the Vitez Brigade. You didn't cease being a soldier, you just changed brigades.

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't change brigades, because the Vitez Brigade didn't exist at the time. It was a sort of battalion, not the Viteska Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot take that any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dealing with your cousin, he was also a soldier, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed --

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the time that he died on the 16th of April, he was a soldier.

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed, he was a sergeant at that time, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps you'd like to look at this document --

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: -- I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- 2828. See, we have here a record of his death. There's his name, parents' name, date of birth; occupation, locksmith; died in Novaci, Vitez, on the front line during an attack by a sniper's bullet.

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then "sergeant" is there.

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What unit was he a member of?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: He was a member of the Vitezovi. I don't know what his rank was. I don't remember that he was a sergeant. I knew that he was a soldier belonging to the Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. In any event -- no, that's fine. The battalion that you say you were a member of, that's the 2nd Battalion of the Tomasevic Brigade, was to become the 1st Battalion of the Viteska Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: The 1st Battalion of the Vitez Brigade, no. It remained the 2nd Battalion. Now, later on, with the creation of the so-called Vitez Brigade, I don't really know, I don't remember that. I don't know those facts --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: -- and how everything evolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I come on to 1993, just a couple of questions about 1992. You've been talking about Kalinska Street. That's in Novi Travnik; correct?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You apparently joined up not on the 8th of April, when your cousin died, of 1992, but you say the 16th of April, 1992. Did you intend to give that as the date that you joined up the Tomasevic Brigade, the 16th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I joined the municipal staff, and that moved to the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade. When and how, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Were you a member of that brigade by June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember dates very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On your way to the front line, you had to pass through Novi Travnik, unless you took a route round it, and this is where you say --

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- you encountered problems in Kalinska Street. First of all, were you in Novi Travnik in June of 1992 during what's been known as the first conflict in Novi Travnik? Were you there then?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why, because you were never going to the front line then?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't in Travnik at all, Novi Travnik, either up at the front line or in town. I was at home at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. You've told us about these problems you encountered in Kalinska Street.

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was this at the time of the second conflict in Novi Travnik in October of 1992; namely, on the 19th of October, or thereabouts?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, there were - how shall I put it - there were those provocations and incidents that took place. And then the barricades were set up and you had to pass those barricades. That's when the incidents took place that I talked about. And they were just provocations, verbal abuse, no weapons involved. That kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the HVO attack on Novi Travnik in the Kalinska Street area in October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Let's just move on to 1993. By February of 1993, if you can remember, what unit were you a member of then? February of 1993.

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: February 1993, the Vitez Battalion, HVO Vitez Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps you would just be good enough to look at a document coming your way, 463. In fact, I don't think you need look at it unless you read English. We'll lay it on the ELMO, and there's one short passage that I'm going to read to see if you agree with it. And as this is in English, I will just read out the relevant couple of lines very slowly and you can hear it in your own language. This is a military information document from one of the international units there dated the 13th of February of 1993. And of your area, it says there's been a number of changes. That Borivoje Malbasic, commander of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade, has now been relieved of his command and has moved to Vares and Mario Cerkez, the former deputy, is now commanding Novi Travnik and Vitez, and the new deputy commander is a man called Sabljic. Does that agree with your recollection of things that there was a time in February 1993 when Mario Cerkez was commanding both the Tomasevic Brigade and also Vitez?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. See if you know something about this fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can he look, please, at Z505 which I've got conveniently marked, because it's a big document. It's the green tabs at the bottom. That's the original for him and that's for the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, this is a listing of HVO members out -- we need the whole title in so we can go out a little bit. That's about it and then we can probably still read it. This is a list of HVO members for Novi Travnik, for the unit and the platoon and the troop. I'm afraid I can't read it now myself here and I've forgotten it's the 2nd Platoon of the 2nd Troop of the 2nd Battalion, and your name is down there. There are two Fabijan Zuljevics, but you are -- you see number 32 on the original and 34? Do you see those names there? They are very hard to see. On the original, Mr. Zuljevic, you can see them on the original on the piece of paper in front of you. And I've put a little green mark by the side of what I think may be your name. Now, which are you, Zuljevic (Drago) Fabijan or Zuljevic (Franjo) Fabijan?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Zuljevic Drago Fabijan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that shows that you were, in the 27th of February, I think the date is, it's not shown at the moment, but never mind, of 1993, you are a deputy captain or a platoon commander. And that's accurate, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No. No. Platoon commander cannot be deputy captain. These were -- there was a coordinator between the two of us and these ranks were not established yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Well, that may be an interpretation or translation error which we needn't trouble with. What you certainly were was a platoon commander and you were in the 2nd Battalion of the Zrinjski Brigade and you were a soldier working in --

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us about it then.

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: In the Zrinjski Brigade? I was not in the Zrinjski Brigade. That's not true, not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then which battalion were you now a member of, 27th of February 1993?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Viteska Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that there's no doubt about it, by February of 1993, the Viteska Brigade existed and was sufficiently well formed that it had organised platoons and platoon commanders. That's your understanding of the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I came to understand that the Vitez Brigade was established in 1993, between April and May. I think that's what I said. The battalion existed up until February but not the brigade. I don't remember the date Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of when the brigade actually came -- was established officially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wanted to intervene as to the manner the questions were being put because for the fourth time, the Prosecutor has asked the question assuming that the Vitez Brigade existed. However, the witness answered for the fourth time running that at that time, the Vitez Brigade did not exist but the Viteska Battalion as a component part of the Stjepan Tomasevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm concerned to know what this witness' understanding was and he's told us that. If he says it's the Viteska Battalion, I'm happy with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Viteska Battalion was sufficiently well formed in February of 1992 that it had organised platoons and organised platoon commanders, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No. There were no platoon commanders. I was not a platoon commander. I was selected and chosen, that is to say, I headed the group. I was not a platoon commander because there were no ranks of that kind. There was no platoon commander. But it was treated as a platoon commander, that is to say, more a coordinator. Some of them were captains. They were coordinators coordinating for the purposes of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you because it may be my mistake for using 1992. This document relates to February of 1993, and that's what I'm asking you about and my mistake because I did use the words 1992. In 1993, as we can see from this document, affairs were sufficiently well organised that there were, on any reckoning, platoon commanders or people in charge of platoons, that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I say again there were no platoon commanders; there were no platoons. They were people from the villages who took shifts on the lines facing the Serbs. We did not expect, that is to say, we were not preparing for a war with the Muslims. And the Vitez Brigade didn't exist at all at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, can you explain this document to us? It was provided, I think, by defendants in another case in this building. Can you explain this document that has your name on it? Can you explain it to us, please?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, could that question be explained to me better? I'm not quite clear on what you mean and what this document means.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Here's a document coming from the HVO that sets out platoons and troops and battalions --

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- all right? It's got your name on it and it says you're a platoon commander. The date of the document is apparently the 27th of February, 1993. Now, are you able to help us, please, explain this document and understand this document?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I have tried to explain the document. I don't know how else to explain it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. The witness has, of course, the B/C/S version in front of him, and I'm hoping that he has been following that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps you'd just better help us with 653, a quick look at that again. It's the same point, Mr. Zuljevic. Just have a look at this document very quickly. It's the top part of the document that relates to your area. This is a document of the 14th of April that gives personnel of the 1st Battalion of the Viteska Brigade by village, and your area is, of course, Dubravica and thereabouts; 19 soldiers in Dubravica in the 1st Company under Slavko Papic. Can you explain this document to us, please? What does the 19 soldiers in Dubravica mean?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: This isn't 19 soldiers, it's 19 people who were, as we call them, members of the HVO, who went on shifts. And those persons were on the list which was to provide the shifts at Slatka Vode or Strikanci. They weren't soldiers. They were soldiers when they were up at the defence lines, but when they came home they were civilians. They went about their business at home, their civilian business.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you one of these 19, please, Mr. Zuljevic?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You remember I asked you right at the beginning this afternoon whether you started off being a soldier and whether you carried on being a soldier till the end of the conflict. Do you remember my asking you that?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. But I claim -- I still claim the following: When we went to Slatka Vode, a soldier was the only -- only the people up at the front line, they were soldiers. When those people went home, and I'm talking about myself, and all of us, we were ordinary civilians. We weren't in charge of anything, or responsible to Slavko Papic or the HVO or anything. We were civilians. And then a shift would come up again, we would go up to the front line, we would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. I have one more question on this document. Just look at the bottom of the entry for the 1st Company Commander, Slavko Papic. It says: "There is a gun missing in the company and there are four sokac and one dobosar gun." Who was making a tally, a record, for the Viteska Brigade of the weaponry of these village members, or whatever they were?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: For the villagers? Well, it might have been Slavko, Slavko Papic, nobody else, for those villages. The coordinator; nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. It was all organised, what you were doing, by the HVO, wasn't it, and by the Viteska Brigade by this time?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, could that question be put clearer, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. The organisation of the people going to the front line was dealt with by the Viteska Brigade on behalf of the HVO, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No, not the Vitez Brigade. It didn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. Very well. You say that you simply left the line where you were engaged on the night of the 15th/16th, leaving equipment behind you; is that really your evidence?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I left the equipment partially, and when I withdrew from the line -- on my own initiative, I left the line, because a scout, as I mentioned a moment ago, told me that the war was in Vitez. I visited Vilenica and withdrew the following day from the front line facing the Serbs. And I took with me some small arms, because the rifles that were there, up at the front line, and the ammunition, all that stayed over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is this the war that you were all looking forward to being involved in, the war with the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No. We did not expect war at all with the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, then, why did you suddenly leave a front line which had apparently needed your service?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I've just said, on my own bat, at my own initiative, I left the line --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But why?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: -- how would you feel if -- well, because it was a question of my family, my wife, my children. You know the mixed composition of the population in Vitez, and how could I be up there when they were down there, and leave my children and somebody having them ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, now, you told us a little bit, and I'm not going to go through it, of what happened by way of defence of the area where you were fighting. Who was in charge of that defence, or was it just a random collection of village guards?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the village guards -- nobody. It came from no one. It wasn't that anybody imposed this on us. These village guards were on our own initiative, that is to say, the war started in 1991, and for the stability of the village, to prevent bandits from coming, I don't know, all those that existed, and the looting of the village and everything. I explained that we even had Serbs up above Krizancevo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How long do you say to this Court you village guards were simply acting without any coordination by the Viteska Brigade? Until what date, roughly?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, from the first day, with the proclamation of the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So what suddenly happened on the first day, whatever day you say that was, what happened on that day that suddenly made you a part of the Viteska Brigade?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: The Viteska Brigade was not in existence yet. The Vitez Brigade was formed in April or May, or perhaps June 1993. I don't really have all this documentation available to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you aware that you've got to suggest to this Court that the Vitez Brigade was formed very late in 1993? Is that what you're responding to, Mr. Zuljevic?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I think, as I have just said, that if this Vitez Brigade existed, then it was formed, perhaps, in 1994 -- that is, 1993. And I also explained it later on that we were issued those cards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, let's have a look at the document 790.1, please. I think the last of three documents, and then I'm done. This is a document from Mario Cerkez, dated the 23rd of April of 1993; it's headed "The Vitez Brigade"; do you see that, Mr. Zuljevic?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It says: "Early in the morning of 23 April 1993, an attack was carried out with ... mortar from Bukve against Jardol village. "The artillery preparation was in itself a sign of an impending infantry attack by the Muslim forces. "At 1200 hours an attack was carried out from Tolovici against Krizancevo Selo and Dubravica. ... artillery preparation, and then an infantry attack followed. ... firing from the Lazine area ..." Now, this is the incident about which you've given evidence, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No. On the 23rd of April. Early in the morning on the 23rd of April 1993, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Weren't you there at that time?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, what I wanted your comment on is this --

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It goes on to talk about the attack and it says, "We have a few men wounded and one missing." It deals with the details of the firing including from what it calls "...The sower of death, the M-84 machine-gun, most active in the Barin Gaj area." And it goes on to say that, "Our units did not immediately return fire but we opened fire on the aforesaid areas," and deals with the sighting of UNPROFOR on Kuber. This is a record of the Vitez Brigade fighting in your area. You were all members of the Vitez Brigade, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No, we were members of the HVO. As I have said, the Vitez Brigade if it was formed, was formed in the March, April, May. And I repeat, I know nothing about this document, the attack on Jardol. I don't recall it at all. I don't know all these facts, when it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have a look at another document very shortly, you may be able to help us with this from your knowledge, 836.2. It's a longer document but I only want your comment on a couple of lines on it. If we stay with page one to begin with, towards the top in the English, top half in any event. This is a document dated the 27th of April from Mario Cerkez. It says, "Situation on the Defence Lines", and the two points I want your help with are these, the first sentence or the first two sentences read as follows: "Further to your request of the 27th of April, we inform you of the following: The Vitez Brigade's zone of responsibility is divided into five defence sectors." Mr. Zuljevic, those sectors, were those reflected by the battalions that were formed within the brigade?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: They were formed in villages as villages defended themselves, so the areas of responsibility were defined. At that time, perhaps there was a brigade, but it could not concern any battalions because the HVO did not have any battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My question simply is: Did the sectors that were being spoken of here, the 27th of April, did they become reflected in or did they indeed become battalions?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: These were already the defence lines for Vitez and then divided into sectors. I don't really know much about this document but I shall help us as much as I can. And now I am talking about where I was. We held the sector, it is from Vjetrenica road to the Krcevine Bridge, if you can call it a sector, but those were mostly people from the village that were there, you know, on those defence lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, if you'd now like to turn to the last page, page three, about eight lines up from the bottom, and in the English version to the second sheet, the last three lines, last four lines. In this document by Mr. Cerkez, the last part reads as follows: "In spite of the difficulties that we have outlined in this matter, our assessment is that the achieved defence lines are being firmly held and we are ready to successfully defend all features that are under HVO control although a need is being felt for greater logistical support primarily in terms of ammunition." Then over the page, "There is also a need for greater cooperation with units of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade of Novi Travnik in order to prevent the penetration of Muslim forces from the direction of Novi Travnik, the villages of Opara and Rostovo towards Kruscica." Now, this report shows clearly, Mr. Zuljevic, that what you were doing from the moment this fighting began was coordinated work on behalf of the Vitez Brigade; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just still the random work of village guards?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No. Here there were already lines. We were talking about lines being held, but those lines had already been taken when the war broke out on the 16th. Then we came out and dug in at those lines. Those lines never moved except that some of them fell, but as for the rest towards Novi Travnik and all that up there, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Last document, 819.2. You tell us, Mr. Zuljevic, that the Muslims left the village of Novaci; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And did you see any of their going?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about their going?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No. All I know is what I heard in the morning that they had come out or pulled out, as I said in that -- what's it. That is, that they pulled out, that they left because they were safer in Mahala than there because it was a road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, if we look at this document, if we look at the second sheet, first of all, we'll see that it's a document of the Vitezovi's commander, Darko Kraljevic. I'm sorry that the original version is not very satisfactorily photocopied, but it's almost all there. But if we come back to the first sheet, we can see under the losses, of the seven dead we can see your cousin's name there, Ivan Zuljevic, killed in the village of Novaci at 0945 hours. But if we go up towards the top of the page, we see for the 18th of April, which would be two days after your cousin died, the village of Novaci was cleansed. Well, now you were there by the 18th.

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No. Not the 18th. Until the 18th I was in front of my house when I came back from the front line. I came on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How far away was Novaci from your house?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, they are my neighbours 200 metres say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, Darko Kraljevic of the famous Vitezovi group recalls cleansing a village 200 metres from your house on a day you're there. Can you tell us something about it, please?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't really know much about the Vitezovi. I know that Darko Kraljevic was their commander, but all the formations that they belonged to, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Zuljevic, I hope I made it clear. This is an event whereby a whole village - or however you describe Novaci, hamlet - a whole village left their homes and it appears that the Vitezovi did it by cleansing the area 200 metres from your door. Will you please tell us what happened?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Who? As far as I knew, there was not any significant fighting in Novaci or any massacres or some major fighting or any losses. But what happened on the 16th, that was the only time when that happened, but I wasn't there on the 16th so I cannot say anything about that. And when I came, that woman, the neighbour who was right next there and stayed there and then they went to Mahala. And I can say who that lady is. It is Zaida who spent there another two or three days and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you aware of women in Novaci being mistreated, indeed, being mistreated as badly as women can be, Witness S is the relevant witness, being raped? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No. No. I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, although you weren't there, you say, on the 16th of April, did you hear of shells falling on Novaci on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't remember about any shells falling. I was -- when I was there on the 17th there were no shells. About the 16th, I don't know. I didn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That was Dr. Mujezinovic's evidence, Your Honour. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think that is correct and I don't think that we ever heard any evidence about any crimes in Novaci.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
