utterances.text: We most certainly did. There is reference, as my recollection is, of a complaint. It was not direct evidence, it was evidence of a complaint to a doctor. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That is correct, but --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's the basis of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I would like -- I would like to stress now that the witness is faced with so-called evidence like category, and he might have been confused. He wasn't, but he might have. It is not fair practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's perfectly fair. There was a suggestion that some women had been raped in Novaci. It went no more than that, and the Prosecutor was entitled to put it to the witness, since he was in the area, did he know anything about it, and he says he didn't. So there it is. It doesn't take the case any further. Yes. Any re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zuljevic, you were shown document 505 relating to February 1993. I will ask you the following: Do you recall if, in February 1993, you were on duty doing your shift at Slatka Vode?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: During your testimony, you repeatedly used the term the Vitez Battalion. Will you please tell us what unit -- within what unit, within what formation did the Vitez Battalion operate?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Stjepan Tomasevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But this name, the Vitez Battalion, Viteska Bojna, it described the composition of those troops because those were principally people from Vitez, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zuljevic, when taking your shifts at Slatka Vode and Sljivcica, were you always the one who led the group or were there different leaders of the group?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: There were different leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At times it was you, and at times it was somebody else?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you did not have a permanent duty of the group leader or the platoon as it was put to you here?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You were asked, Mr. Zuljevic, how is it that you abandoned the front line on the 16th, or rather on the 18th of April after you learned that the war had broken out in the area of Vitez and after you had learned that some of your relatives had been killed. My question is as follows: Was it more important for you to remain at the defence line against the JNA or protect your wife and your children?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, to protect my wife and my children, no doubt about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And after you returned to the village, you said that some defence lines had been defined and you described it to them; is that correct? Is it correct to say that those defence lines were in point of fact above your houses and were there to he defend your village?

utterances.speaker: FABIJAN ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Zuljevic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Zuljevic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just a word before we are continuing with the next witness. I am a little bit worried because of one fact. So far, at least it is how I understood, the fact that Viteska Brigade was founded during the March 1993 was not disputed. And I would like to remind the Court and my dear colleagues from the other side that we did make that statement also in pre-trial brief, and we accepted that Cerkez was a commander of that brigade from the beginning, from the foundation of that brigade. It seems that there is a dispute now. If there is a dispute, we then have to consider, despite of the fact that the evidence about foundation of the brigade is already submitted in the form of documents, but we have to then consider also the witnesses on that fact. Indeed, some witnesses already testified about that, but it seems that it is irrelevant now for the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think there is any dispute about it. The essential question is how well organised was it in April 1993. Now, as far as I know, that's the issue which the Court has to determine. Was it an organised brigade of some sort or was it totally disorganised? These are matters you have to concern yourself with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour, and that is how I understood the situation until --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, until we hear differently, that is the way we propose to proceed unless we hear to the contrary. Can we go on now?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I might just raise one question about the Exhibit Z819.2. On page two of the document, it says that concerning the PPN Vitezovi, "It is best that you read the written commendation of the commander of the headquarters Operative Zone Central Bosnia, Mr. Colonel Tihomir Blaskic, which I have enclosed for you to view." I wonder if we might just request a copy of the enclosure it seems to be a document of some significance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If I've got a copy of the document, I'll make it available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let's have the next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Tomic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On behalf of Mr. Cerkez's Defence, I shall be asking you some questions based on your statement, and I should like to ask you to try to recall the events the best you can so as to help the Court, and us, of course. At the same time, I should also like to ask you to pause between my questions and your answers so as to facilitate the interpreter's work. Now, would you be so kind and tell us, for the record, what is your full name, your place and date of birth?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 10th of December, 1959, in Dubravica, municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You are a Croat by ethnicity; you're of Roman Catholic faith, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You are a citizen of both the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You are married and you have three sons.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You are a carpenter by profession.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You are not employed.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You came out of the vocational school in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, as a result of the events which happened during this war, you have become an invalid and you have a recognised disability of 68 per cent, is it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are you a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness speak up, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, you were asked by the interpreters, could you speak up a bit or speak a bit closer to the microphones so we can hear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What party did you belong to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the HSP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The HSP is the party which means the Croat Party of Rights, is it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So this is the party with the longest political tradition in that area insofar as the Croat people are concerned, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It dates back to the last century, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, when the war started in Croatia, when the JNA attacked first Slovenia and then Croatia, did the Croat Party of Rights form some armed units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What were these units of the HSP called?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: HOS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Those combat units participated in the resistance against the JNA attack.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In Bosnia-Herzegovina, were such units formed as well?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are you aware, in view of the ethnic makeup, who were the members of those HOS units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us if in 1991/1992 the number of Muslims was large or insignificant? What would you say?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Almost half of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, before the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you worked abroad, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You worked in Austria, in Switzerland, and in Germany, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When is it that you decided to go and work abroad?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: After I returned from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And that was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: The first time, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, do go on.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: The first time, I think, in 1982, or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: From your area, did any other people go and become migrant workers, or were you an exception?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: There were very many people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But, of course, you came home from time to time.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you knew what was going on.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When did you come home for good to Bosnia, from your work in Germany? What year?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: In 1990 -- well, it was, in fact, late 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That was the time when war had broken out already in Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you have a special motive for returning to the country at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what led you to come home? What was your motive?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, I wanted to go to Croatia to fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will ask you again: Were you an exception, was your motive exceptional, or did some others working abroad come back for the same reason?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: A lot of people did the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And it was then, on your return, as far as I understand, that you joined the Croatian Party of Rights.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you stayed in your village and lived there.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Later on during 1991, what were your thoughts about the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Did you think there would not be a war, or did you think something else?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: No. There were signs that it would spread to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What did you do then?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, then, I don't know the exact date, but I set off to Croatia. In Zenica, however, I was stopped by the civil police and prevented from doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You set out to Croatia with the intention of joining the fight against the JNA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Why were you prevented in doing this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, you did not manage to do this, so you returned home.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What did you do after that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Then I joined the reserve police force in order to gain access to weapons, because I had to defend myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At that time, Mr. Tomic, what was the ethnic makeup of the reserve police force? Was it just Croats or were there other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: There were Croats and Muslims, mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you remember who the chief of police was at that time in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: I think it was Mr. Skopljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Which Skopljak?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Pero. Pero.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And after him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I were to suggest to you it was Mirko Samija, could you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What were the relations in the reserve police force? How did they develop over time? From the middle of 1992 onwards, what were the relations between the Croats and the Muslims in the reserve police force?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, they parted ways; that's how I would describe it. There were tensions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, can you illustrate this by an example? How did they part ways? What was it the Muslims or the Croats did to cause this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, there were various rumours, various conversations. They said, "Well, another 500 years of Muslim rule will come about," things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you conclude from what they said that your Muslim colleagues wanted to establish a state of their own?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: They said, "We will play the first half of the match together with you, but the second half against you, because we are going to build up a Dzamahirija here."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, in your understanding, what does the word "Dzamahirija" mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: I think that that is an Islamic state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was that acceptable to you personally, this kind of thinking?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, of course not. It wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. You were in the reserve police force; you described how this happened. In September 1992, at the beginning of the autumn, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Then I went over to the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you remember who was the commander of the military police at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: At that time I think it was Mr. Marijan Jukic or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Or?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Vlado Santic, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you're not sure.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you undergo any training or any specialised training for a military policeman?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Pasko Ljubicic sent us to Neum for a month's training.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: For the sake of clarity, Mr. Tomic, where is Neum, the town of Neum?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: It's in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that you spent about a month in training.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, about 28 days. I'm not sure exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After that you went back; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you became a member of the military police, and before that you were in the reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: While you were still in the reserve police force, what were your duties? What activities did you perform?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, for a long time, together with the Muslims, we manned a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. checkpoint. But only with the Croats I went to the defence lines against the Serbs, because the mayor of Jajce - I can't remember his name now - would come to fetch us. And we went with the soldiers doing shifts, for example, to Jajce, to Turbe, to other places, to the line facing the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you were, in fact, used for combat activities as a reserve civil policeman; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Tomic, that other people from Vitez, volunteers, used to come to the Jajce front?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know who organised them to go to the defence line against the JNA and the Bosnian Serb army? Who organised them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You were sent to defend Jajce by the reserve police force; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At the invitation of the mayor of Jajce.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The other people you mentioned who went there from Vitez as volunteers, who sent them? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: They were sent by the municipal staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said that you participated in the fighting to defend Jajce and that you also manned certain checkpoints on the roads.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Tomic, what were these checkpoints, and why had they been set up? What was their purpose? We are talking about 1992, the second half of that year, of course.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, as a member of the military police by that time, I was at the crossroads between Travnik and Novi Travnik. We checked the passage of people, goods, and so on, and this was our only task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At that time you did this together with the Muslims; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: In late 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The second half of 1992.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So the checkpoints were already single-ethnic checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, November 1992, this is an important month in your life.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened to you personally in November 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. On the 22nd of November, at about midnight, we were on our way back from the checkpoint, I and six colleagues of mine ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, go on.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: We were stationed in Kruscica, in the Ribnjak Hotel. Then we came across a Muslim police patrol in Kruscica. They stopped us and recognised us; they asked us what was new and let us through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So they stopped you at a checkpoint held by the Muslim armed forces.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the Muslim police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And then you went on.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: After about a kilometre we came across a group of people, 30 to 40 of them perhaps, who closed off the road, and we got out to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you say a group of men, were they civilians or were they wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: They were in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were they soldiers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where was this? What is the name of that place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Fatina Vodica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That's the area of Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What happened next after you stopped?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Then they cocked their rifles; they all had automatic rifles. They said that we should get out of the car, lie down face down, put our hands behind our heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you. Among the soldiers who stopped you, did you manage to recognise anyone? Were they local people? Did you recognise any of them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: I recognised quite a few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were there people among them whom you could not recognise?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: I think there were Mujahedin because they had beards and they were in black, and they were dark skinned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So they threatened you with weapons and made you lie face down and put your hands behind your heads?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did they disarm you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, they disarmed us. They took our weapons and everything we had including our rings, chains, watches and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In fact, they robbed you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What about the military insignia on your uniforms?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: They tore them off. As for the badges, they took them away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you were treated like this. What happened next?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Then we went to a sort of garage. They brought us there together, and together we were left there. I remember there was a very strong light in front. So they called us out by name, one by one, and took us out to be tortured.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How did they know your names?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: There were so many of them, I think at least 15 of them were people we had known for 20, 25 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, practically, they were your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said they took you out of the garage one by one. What happened outside?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Whoever went outside, we heard screams, blows with all sorts of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And could you see from the garage what was going on outside?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You only heard the sounds.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, and the screams.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you concluded from this what?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, what was going on, that they were being beaten mercilessly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did they take you out of that garage?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can remember twice, and I can't say any more. They treated me like an object.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What did they do to you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, they -- the first time when I went out, they beat me up well. The second time, they hit me in the face with rifle butt of a machine-gun, and after that, I don't remember anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You lost consciousness?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What did they beat you with?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, with bats, rifle butts, they punched us, kicked us. They used whatever they could lay their hands on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did they say anything to you? Did they ask anything of you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: They cursed our Ustasha mothers. They asked why we were wearing those uniforms. They said that that would be a Dzamahirija and while I am still conscious I said to a former colleague of mine, "Why are you establishing a Dzamahirija when it doesn't exist anywhere properly and you can't build a Dzamahirija on my fatherland."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said they cursed your Ustasha mothers and they asked you why you were wearing those uniforms and they tore the insignia off your uniforms. What sort of patch did you have?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that you were beaten with the rifle butt of a machine-gun and that you lost consciousness as a result; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What injuries did you sustain?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: I had fractures of my jaw, upper and lower jaw, a broken nose, cheek bones, skull fractures, legs, and all sorts of other injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And the result of that was that you are a 60 per cent invalid; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were you injured in the eye area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you suffer from that today?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: I suffer a great deal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, I have frequent -- very bad headaches. My circulation is poor, and I feel faint. I don't see. My eyesight isn't very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you lost consciousness, you said. When did you come to, regain consciousness?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, I regained consciousness in the hospital in Nova Bila some ten days later, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you were transported to the hospital in Nova Bila from Kruscica, how did you get there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't conscious, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did they tell you about how you were transferred to hospital?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, I heard later on that a colleague of mine who was also seriously injured, he was all -- he suffered from knife wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you say colleague, he was amongst the six military policemen?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were you visited by your relatives in hospital, your family?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: But nobody could recognise me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Not even my own father or brothers or sisters or children recognised me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Why didn't they recognise you? Did you have your face bandaged?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've got the point really, Mr. Mikulicic. Can we move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the hospital in Nova Bila undergoing treatment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I didn't stay on long. Once I had returned consciousness, soon after that, I was transferred from Nova Bila to Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you continued your treatment there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Tomic, who was in the hospital room with you in Split?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, there were four of us. Two Croats and two Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Members of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Otherwise at the hospital in Split in Croatia, were there Muslims, members of the BH army there for treatment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you notice that the medical staff and doctors had a different attitude to them as opposed to you Croats?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How long did you spend in the Split hospital undergoing treatment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: After a month had gone by or thereabouts, we listened to the radio and tensions were increasing all the time. I decided to ask the doctor if I could go home. He said I couldn't, but then I left hospital at my own responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Actually, you escaped from hospital, did you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you went back home, to your own house in your village?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What did you do there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, several days later, that is to say, I spent some days at home, and then I went to the police, to the command to report, to say that I had arrived, that I was back home. But they said, "You stay at home. Go back home. You're all -- you need treatment. So have some treatment at home. Rest up a bit and recuperate." So I went back home and I got better slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But then you ended up in hospital again, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Once again in Nova Bila?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Nova Bila. And I got fed up with that too because I wasn't able to take all the lying down. The Serbs were relatively close by, and you could hear them breaking through the defence lines now and again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And then you decided to leave the hospital; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you went back to the command of the military police and reported there for duty?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, and they once again told me to go home and they said when the need arose, they would come and call me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And how long did you stay at home that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't go back to the military police until the end of September 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That means when the armed conflict broke out in Vitez and the surroundings on the 16th of April. Were you at home then?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What did you do then when the conflict occurred?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, I heard detonations, strong explosions. That was what woke me. I got up, went out and saw everything burning, everything on fire. Everybody was already awake in the house. I took up my rifle. I said to my wife, "There's something wrong. You stay indoors and I'll go outside to see what's going on." Below my house, I met several neighbours and I talked to them. We saw that Vitez was being shelled. We didn't know if it was the Serbs shelling or whether they had already entered Vitez. But they told me that we ought to go to Lazine, which is a little way off from my house, about a kilometre away. Lazine, that's where we went. When we got there, we came across some of my neighbours and we started making up a defence line there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What did your neighbours tell you? Who was it who was --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, they said that the Muslims had attacked us and that we had to organise ourselves until somebody more capable turned up, somebody who would be able to organise us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: These neighbours of yours, the ones that you went to Lazine with, did they have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, not all of them, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were they members of the village guards in your village?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that you went outside and saw everything burning. Did you mean that there was actual fire or did you mean it figuratively?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: No, figuratively, that is to, say hundreds of projectiles were flying about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And that's the term you use, is it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Later on, you were wounded again, were you not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When was that and where?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: I think it was in mid-August at Lazine. I was wounded when a grenade fell from the BH army positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you went for treatment again?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: No, I was at home. I stayed at home for 10 or 12 days because I wasn't wounded that badly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what happened next, after you had recovered from that second wounding?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: I went back to Lazine after that. However, at the end of September, I -- that is to say a military policeman came by and told me to report to the 4th Battalion, and Marinko Palavra was already in command of that battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And that's what you did. You reported to the command of the 4th Battalion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, where were you assigned to then?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: I was deployed according to need, that is to say, the commander would make up a schedule, and we were sent to different parts of the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were you deployed for combat activity or did you have some other job to perform, other assignment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, we were in the trenches up at the front line mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As far as you remember, how many people did the military police comprise of at that time, how many men?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as the Vitez -- as Vitez is concerned, 120.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I heard you. What did you say?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: 120. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: 120, thank you. Later on, you ended up undergoing medical treatment again; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. After the war when there was a cease-fire, I went to Nova Bila. I felt very ill. We started thinking about the situation when everything was over and wondered what had actually happened. I was feeling very weak, fairly poorly, so I ended up in Split again, and then I was sent to Neum for rehabilitation and I spent about three months there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you ever meet Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How long have you known him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, I've known him for a long time, since we were kids.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you meet him during your school days?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know him from elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know his family?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How would you describe his family?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: They're ordinary, normal citizens, well-behaved, well brought up, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was Mario Cerkez's family known to be a family that liked quarrelling?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear Mario Cerkez or anybody from his family say anything bad about Muslims, or any other members of national minorities apart from Croats?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you ever Mario Cerkez drink? Was he prone to alcohol or brawls or anything of that kind?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic has no questions for this witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I heard what Your Honour was saying. I'd much prefer to do it tomorrow morning, if it's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No doubt, but we want a reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. It's been a question of opportunities for preparation. There have been a number of witnesses and, as you've seen, I've been dealing with them all this week.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Provided it's done expeditiously, you can have the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, we are going to adjourn now until tomorrow morning. Would you be back, please, at half past nine tomorrow, and would you remember not to talk to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include members of the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we part and just so that I don't forget - nothing to do with this witness - Mr. Sayers' request for the enclosure that I said we would search for, we have been searching for it, well, others have, and apparently we don't possess it. So there it is. I'll just confirm that myself overnight, but that appears to be the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now. Half past nine tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
